paragraphs: Alyosha stood undecided for a while after hearing the order his father shouted to him from the carriage. But for all his uneasiness, he did not stand still. That was not his way. He went straight to the kitchen to find out what his father had been doing upstairs. Then he set off, trusting that somewhere along the way he would find an answer to the doubt that troubled him. I should add at once that his father’s shouts, ordering him home “with his mattress and pillow,” did not frighten him in the least. He understood perfectly well that those domineering shouts were only “a flourish,” done for effect. In the same way, a tradesman in our town, celebrating his name-day with a party of friends, got angry when he was refused more vodka. He smashed his own crockery and furniture, tore his own clothes and his wife’s, and finally broke his own windows, all for the sake of effect. Next day, of course, when he was sober, he was sorry about the broken cups and saucers. Alyosha knew that his father would let him go back to the monastery next day, maybe even that evening. Besides, he was fully convinced that his father might hurt anyone else, but would never hurt him. Alyosha was certain that no one in the whole world would ever want to hurt him, and what is more, he knew that no one could. This was, for him, an axiom, accepted once and for all without question, and he went on his way without hesitating, relying on it.

But at that moment a different kind of anxiety troubled him, and it worried him all the more because he could not put it into words. It was fear of a woman, of Katerina Ivanovna, who had begged him so urgently, in the note Madame Hohlakov handed to him, to come and see her about something. The request, and the need to go, had at once stirred an uneasy feeling in his heart. All morning the feeling had grown more and more painful, in spite of the scenes at the hermitage and at the Father Superior’s. It was not that he was uneasy because he did not know what she would speak of, or what he ought to answer. And he was not afraid of her simply because she was a woman. He knew little of women, but he had spent his whole life with women, from early childhood until he entered the monastery. He was afraid of that woman, Katerina Ivanovna. He had been afraid of her from the first time he saw her. He had seen her only two or three times, and had happened to say only a few words to her. He thought of her as a beautiful, proud, commanding girl. It was not her beauty that troubled him, but something else. And the vagueness of his dread made the dread itself greater. The girl’s aims were of the noblest, he knew that. She was trying to save his brother Dmitri, out of pure generosity, though Dmitri had already behaved badly to her. Yet although Alyosha recognized all these fine and generous feelings and gave them their due, a shiver began to run down his back as soon as he came near her house.

He reflected that he would not find Ivan, who was such a close friend of hers, there with her, for Ivan was certainly with their father by now. He was even more certain not to find Dmitri there, and he had a foreboding of the reason. So his talk would be with her alone. He had a great longing to run and see his brother Dmitri before that fateful interview. He could talk to him about it without showing him the letter. But Dmitri lived a long way off, and was sure to be out too. He stood still for a minute and reached a final decision. Crossing himself with a quick, habitual gesture, and smiling at once, he turned resolutely toward his terrible lady.

He knew her house. If he went by the High Street and then across the market-place, it was a long way round. Our town is small, but it is spread out, and the houses are far apart. And meanwhile his father was expecting him, and perhaps had not yet forgotten his order. He might be unreasonable, so Alyosha had to hurry to get there and back. So he decided to take a short cut by the back way, for he knew every inch of the ground. That meant skirting fences, climbing over hurdles, and crossing other people’s back-yards, where everyone he met knew him and greeted him. This way he could reach the High Street in half the time.

He had to pass the garden next to his father’s, which belonged to a little tumbledown house with four windows. The owner of this house, as Alyosha knew, was a bedridden old woman, who lived with her daughter. The daughter had been a genteel maid-servant in generals’ families in Petersburg. She had now been home for a year, looking after her sick mother. She always dressed up in fine clothes, though she and her old mother had sunk into such poverty that they went every day to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen for soup and bread, which Marfa gave them readily. Yet although the young woman came up for soup, she had never sold any of her dresses, and one of them even had a long train. Alyosha knew this from Rakitin, who always knew everything that was going on in the town. He had forgotten it as soon as he heard it. But now, on reaching the garden, he remembered the dress with the train. He raised his head, which had been bowed in thought, and came upon something quite unexpected.

Over the hurdle in the garden, Dmitri, standing on something, was leaning forward, waving his arms wildly and beckoning to him. He was obviously afraid to say a word for fear of being overheard. Alyosha ran up to the hurdle.
“It’s a good thing you looked up. I was nearly shouting to you,” Mitya said in a joyful, hurried whisper. “Climb in here quickly! How splendid that you’ve come! I was just thinking of you!”

Alyosha was delighted too, but he did not know how to get over the hurdle. Mitya put his strong hand under his elbow to help him jump. Tucking up his cassock, Alyosha leapt over the hurdle as nimbly as a barefoot street boy.
“Well done! Now come along,” said Mitya in an excited whisper.
“Where?” whispered Alyosha, looking around. He found himself in a deserted garden, with no one near but the two of them. The garden was small, but the house was at least fifty paces away.
“There’s no one here. Why are you whispering?” asked Alyosha.

“Why am I whispering? The deuce take it!” cried Dmitri at the top of his voice. “You see what silly tricks nature plays on a man. I’m here in secret, and on the watch. I’ll explain later. But knowing it’s a secret, I started whispering like a fool, when there’s no need. Let’s go. Over there. Until then, be quiet. I want to kiss you.
Glory to God in the world, Glory to God in me ...
I was just repeating that, sitting here, before you came.”

The garden was about three acres, and trees were planted only along the fence on all four sides. There were apple-trees, maples, limes and birch-trees. The middle of the garden was an empty grass space, from which several hundredweight of hay was carried off in the summer. The garden was rented out for a few roubles for the summer. There were also plantations of raspberries, currants and gooseberries along the sides, and a kitchen garden had recently been planted near the house.

Dmitri led his brother to the most secluded corner of the garden. There, in a thicket of lime-trees and old bushes of black currant, elder, snowball-tree and lilac, stood a tumble-down green summer-house, blackened with age. Its walls were lattice-work, but it still had a roof that could give shelter. God knows when this summer-house was built. There was a tradition that it had been put up some fifty years before by a retired colonel called von Schmidt, who owned the house at that time. It was all falling apart. The floor was rotting, the planks were loose, and the woodwork smelled musty. In the summer-house there was a green wooden table fixed in the ground, and around it were some green benches that were still fit to sit on. Alyosha had noticed at once his brother’s exhilarated state, and on entering the arbor he saw half a bottle of brandy and a wineglass on the table.
“That’s brandy,” Mitya laughed. “I see the look on your face: ‘He’s drinking again!’ Don’t trust the appearance.
Don’t trust the worthless, lying crowd, And put aside your doubts.

I’m not drinking, I’m only ‘indulging,’ as that pig, your Rakitin, says. He’ll be a civil councilor one day, but he’ll always talk about ‘indulging.’ Sit down. I could take you in my arms, Alyosha, and press you to my chest until I crush you, because in the whole world—in reality—in re-al-i-ty—(can you take that in?) I love no one but you!”
He said the last words in a sort of exaltation.

“No one but you, and one ‘jade’ I’ve fallen in love with, to my ruin. But being in love doesn’t mean loving. You can be in love with a woman and still hate her. Remember that! I can still talk about it cheerfully. Sit down here by the table and I’ll sit beside you and look at you, and keep talking. You’ll keep quiet and I’ll keep talking, because the time has come. But on second thought, you know, I’d better speak quietly, because here—here—you never can tell what ears are listening. I’ll explain everything. As they say, ‘the story will be continued.’ Why have I been longing for you? Why have I been thirsting for you all these days, and just now? (It’s five days since I dropped anchor here.) Because you’re the only one I can tell everything to. Because I must, because I need you, because tomorrow I’ll fall from the clouds, because tomorrow life ends and begins. Have you ever felt, have you ever dreamed, of falling down a precipice into a pit? That’s just how I’m falling, but not in a dream. And I’m not afraid, and don’t you be afraid. Well, I am afraid, but I enjoy it. It’s not enjoyment, though, but ecstasy. Damn it all, whatever it is! A strong spirit, a weak spirit, a womanish spirit—whatever it is! Let’s praise nature. Look at the sunshine, how clear the sky is, the leaves are all green, it’s still summer. Four o’clock in the afternoon, and such stillness! Where were you going?”
